We investigate decoding of rank metric codes under the assumption of a symmetric error matrix. Our analysis yields two main conclusions. Firstly, we show that for any rank error, there exists a symmetric error of the same rank that is equirank reduced, providing a potential path for the development of rank metric codes with good asymptotic parameters and a decodable GHS bound, as previously conjectured by Beelen, Marchal, and Oehmke. Secondly, we demonstrate that an interleaved rank error can be effectively decoded by identifying and addressing its locally decodable components, ultimately leading to an improved code rate for the rank metric analogue of the Euclidean asymptotically good family based on the Geometric GRS codes.

Building upon previous work by \cite{Ferrara:1971vh}, \cite{Ferrara:1973vz}, we develop a comprehensive integral representation for conformal block operators in CFT$_2$, specifically tailored for spinning primary fields. Notably, this integral expression can be re-expressed as a product of two weighted AdS$_2$ field combinations when the primary fields in question are conserved, which we demonstrate yields the conserved spin W$_2$ AdS$_2$ field in the relevant theory's spectrum.

Future experiments to study the Cosmic Microwave Background will be able to measure a crucial parameter $r$ with high precision, however a significant challenge lies ahead. Delensing is essential to reduce the noise caused by non-Gaussian non-linear structures formed early in the universe's history. To effectively delense, it is necessary to reconstruct these structures accurately. Our proposed approach utilizes a two-stage neural network system to not only do this but also distinguish between these structures and the primordial tensor perturbations formed in the very early stages of the universe's history. To validate the performance of our neural network system, we formed artificial forecast scenarios, and found that it can reduce the noise caused by these structures to a precise level, allowing for a $r$ measurement with a precision of $0.0015$ for future experiments.

In 1992, Gelfand and MacPherson established a local and combinatorial approach to calculating Pontrjagin classes for differentiable manifolds. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds.

We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN 2020jfo, a Type II-S supernova, from its discovery on 2020 April 13 until day 50 of its evolution. During this period, we identified two distinct phases in its light curve. Initially, the spectrum displayed typical Type II characteristics, but by day 30, it became heavily ionized and then returned to its previous state around day 40. From the start until day 30, the supernova's expansion rate was slower than usual for its kind. From day 40 until day 50, it expanded at a rate more typical of Type Ia supernovae. We also observed a decline in the [O I] 6300, 6330 Å line around day 30, which may have been caused by either increased ionization or a decrease in oxygen within the supernova's outer layers. We also noted that SN 2020jfo, like SN 2006X, had a shorter-than-average plateau in its evolution.

To greatly reduce the number of image sensors required for wide-field X-ray monitoring using lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves grouping multiple lenses within an LE telescope array so that X-ray images formed by different lenses overlap on a single sensor. By employing this setup, we can achieve wide-field monitoring as efficiently as lobster-eye (LE) optics, but with significantly fewer sensors; for example, an MuLE telescope with 10^6 mirrors would only require an equivalent group of 10^5 image sensors. However, this approach does present challenges in terms of spatial resolution and spectral information, which can be recovered at the expense of an MuLE telescope's field of view. Analysis indicates that while an MuLE optics design can effectively detect sources as bright as NGC 1068 and other highly variable objects like TDE AT2019qdg in the SWIFT-JBAT2 catalog, it falls short in resolving point sources and recovering spectral information. We suggest an approach called unmixing in MuLE (UMuLE) imaging that can be implemented with linear deconvolution techniques to restore some of the sacrificed spectral information and partial spatial resolution in an MuLE optics detector's output.

We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations.

To investigate the structure of dark matter, a deep learning framework was implemented and used to explore the impact of velocity and density information on the formation of halos through $N$-body cosmological simulations. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time. Results showed that including velocity information significantly improved prediction accuracy by a factor of 10 when the simulation was resolved at a high $1026^3$ grid, and by a factor of 30 by a factor of 10 when the simulation had fewer simulation particles ($512^3$). At earlier stages of the simulation's evolution, including velocity data had a much smaller effect. Furthermore, models that used both density and velocity information identified substructures better at an intermediate resolution but struggled at higher and lower resolutions. A key finding was that including velocity information at earlier stages of the simulation significantly reduced information entropy, especially for low-mass halos. Based on these results, a novel approach was proposed to study the role of velocity fields in the formation of dark matter halos at various masses and redshifts.

Converting an audio recording of music into a symbolic format is a challenging Music Information Retrieval task, specifically piano transcription. This study proposes a semi-supervised technique using low-rank matrix factorization methods, notably Convolutive Nonnegative Matrix Factorization. Utilizing a single audio recording of each individual note, we demonstrate on the MAPS dataset that our proposed semi-supervised CNMF method surpasses conventional low-rank factorization techniques, but slightly lags behind leading deep learning approaches while facing broader applicability issues.

We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for steady-state configurations, utilizes first-order derivative interpolation within a co-rotating coordinate framework. Nevertheless, this framework induces non-conservative evolution when applied to time-dependent scenarios due to the presence of mass redistribution and angular momentum changes within the stellar body. To circumvent this challenge, we introduce an innovative formulation of the Einstein-equations that preserves the total angular momentum integral, thereby enabling a balanced accounting of angular momentum during non-conservative evolution. This technique paves the way for the simulation of evolving rotating stars by mitigating numerical pollution of gravitational wave signals through precise control of global angular momentum balance. Key features of this approach include a time-dependent angular velocity function, $\Omega(\tau, t)$, and the transformation of specific angular momentum distributions from Lagrangian to Eulerian coordinates. To demonstrate the practical applications of this approach, we employ a simplified one-component equation of state devoid of rotational effects and utilize numerical simulations to examine rotating neutron stars characterized by differential rotation, ultimately revealing persistent over-densities at the star's center following the cessation of axial disk rotation.

A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized framework called a dual-domain dataset, which combines data from two different sources. We've called this framework the Document Pre-Training (DPT) protocol. The DPT protocol allows for the creation of large-scale, high-quality datasets of visually complex documents from two different sets of data, thereby significantly saving time and money in acquiring these datasets. In fact, our experiments show that models trained using the DPT protocol require up to 10 times less data and 6 times less manual labor during the labeling process, resulting in substantial improvements in accuracy across a wide range of tasks including extracting numbers from invoices and matching items from invoices to purchase orders.

The collaborations of the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-Wave Observatory and Virgo have observed the full spectrum of merging compact binaries consisting of binary black hole and binary neutron star events. Researchers have also detected evidence of neutron star-neutron star merging events. Analyzing outcomes from these observations holds significant value for scientific understanding, particularly in determining the fates of merging neutron stars and whether they produce heavy elements. To make this possible, distinguishing characteristics of various signals need to be identified. In this context, we investigate multiple machine learning techniques to simultaneously detect and classify specific features of a neutron star-neutron star merger event based on time-domain analysis of frequency evolution of the chirp signal. Our deep learning model successfully detects and categorizes these characteristics with high accuracy, surpassing traditional statistical extraction methods.

The adverse effects of social determinants of health on the cardiovascular system are well-documented, yet social stigma associated with certain determinants often prevents individuals from seeking necessary cardiovascular care. As cardiovascular disease continues to be the leading cause of mortality in the United States, there is a pressing need for an automated method to identify social determinants of health in clinical notes. In response to this challenge, we developed a two-stage system that utilizes state-of-the-art technology to inject a structural marker into a linear classifier, allowing it to detect specific phrases related to social determinants of health within electronic health records. This innovative approach aims to provide clinicians with a reliable tool to identify patients' social determinants of health directly from clinical notes.

This study is centered on a two-part swimmer known as the scallop, which transitions through varying dynamics across two different fluid environments. We resolve two optimal control scenarios, one focused on achieving the fastest time to relocate the swimmer and another on finding the most energy-efficient method using periodic control to move it between predetermined positions. Leveraging the simplicity provided by limiting switching to one point and taking advantage of the underlying equation's structure, we can divide the problem into manageable components, explicitly solve each part, and consequently derive a comprehensive solution despite the discontinuities. We also utilize numerical modeling to illustrate the efficacy of less frequent switching in minimizing costs for both scenarios.

Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, raising concerns about their long-term social benefits. This study uses a vast dataset of 1.3 million anonymized U.S. urban residents' shopping transactions to analyze how mobility restrictions impacted daily face-to-face encounters and their composition. Findings reveal substantial decreases in the frequency and diversity of urban encounters during the pandemic, which varied across different cities and periods of restricted mobility. Notably, encounter diversity declined more significantly than frequency. By modeling encounter diversity using machine learning, distinct behavioral patterns associated with decreased diversity were identified and linked to specific types of urban encounters. Ultimately, this data-driven approach provides valuable insights for designing public policies that encourage diverse urban interactions, ultimately contributing to broader societal benefits.

Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Instead, it is the impact of colliding disk objects that produces the observed bursts in stellar brightness, along with variations in spectral energy curves and near-infrared light curves. Furthermore, deviations in disk particle distribution can cause variations in infrared light curves, which could potentially be detected by upcoming missions targeting exoplanets.

Buchholz established a practical approach to understanding massless two-dimensional scattering theories. Within this approach, we've demonstrated that a given theory is completely characterized by its asymptotic algebra and scattering matrix under specific conditions. By applying a procedure grounded in von Neumann algebras, we've derived multiple families of interacting wedge-local nets, one of which is closely related to Buchholz-Lechner-Summers' chiral CFT deformation. Using endomorphisms, we've constructed another instance, which is unitarily equivalent to the TQFT obtained from the bulk-disboundary anomaly in three-dimensional free fermi field theory. Furthermore, we've shown that a subset of Buchholz's conditions can be met by a massive fermi field, albeit without a non-degenerate scalar anomaly. Additionally, we've confirmed that chiral anomalies can be present even when the bulk theory is non-anomalous, which can be achieved by altering the boundary condition. Finally, we've explored the connection between our constructions and the gluing of two bulk-to-boundary modules for a massive fermi field, which reflects the contact anomaly.

This study aims to assess 5G cell tower exposures in various critical locations, 
including children's hospitals, medical facilities, schools, and residential areas. 
Cells were modeled using 5G technology at 35 GHz and 28 GHz frequencies, 
and downlink and uplink signals were considered. Exposure levels were calculated 
and mapped for a range of distances from the 5G cell towers, and found to be 
significantly lower near children's hospitals and schools when compared to 
residential buildings. Notably, the maximum exposure levels in children's 
hospitals and schools were 1.5 to 2.5 micro-watts per square meter lower than 
those in residential buildings. Furthermore, given that 5G cell towers will be 
ubiquitous given their anticipated small coverage range, there's a high 
probability of increased children's exposures from 5G cell towers in various 
settings.

This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We examined weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves and performed an asymptotic analysis to describe their long-time dynamics. For constant vorticity flows, we expanded the gravity waves to second-order nonlinearity by using a Hamiltonian Dysthe model. By directly applying Dysthe's Hamiltonian formulation to the water waves with a periodic bottom, we obtained a new water waves Hamiltonian which matches our weakly nonlinear surface gravity waves analysis. This confirms that the local minimum of the Hamiltonian corresponds to the minimum energy state.

In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here.

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing environments demands that mobile robots efficiently navigate complex scenarios. In static settings, robots can use global path planning to navigate, but in dynamic environments with unmarked obstacles, real-time obstacle detection and avoidance become crucial. This paper presents a real-time, sonar-based navigation framework for laptops and other devices that features a layered control system for optimal path finding and smooth navigation around stationary objects and marked rooms. The proposed algorithm allows for efficient, direct routing to targets, minimizing unnecessary detours, and provides modular control, allowing for easy adaptation to new environments and mobile device optimization. A key feature of this system is its ability to navigate directly to targets, even in complex, multi-room settings, by using a combination of sonar data and map information to identify doorways and other passable areas. The algorithm's performance was tested and demonstrated in various environments, from simple, two-room settings to more complex, four-room configurations, using an Intel laptop and a range of sonar sensors.

The prevalence of false news on social media poses a significant problem,
especially for younger individuals who may lack the critical thinking skills to
differentiate between fact and fiction. Research has been conducted to investigate
the efficacy of using text summarization techniques to identify false news. This study
examines whether generating concise versions of news articles can help in
distinguishing between authentic and fabricated stories. We utilize existing
summarization models to create both genuine and fictitious news summaries, then
compare them to original articles to develop effective classification methods.
Our experiments reveal that combining rules-based approaches with machine learning
algorithms, specifically RoBERTa-base, yields optimal results in distinguishing
false news from real stories based on their summaries.

This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical models known as random field systems. The study focuses on a specific aspect of these systems – how the geometry of their underlying space influences the systems' overall behavior. The investigation involves the statistical properties of these systems when they are confined to curved surfaces in a probabilistic setting. The results show that the system's overall stability is significantly impacted by the curved surface's properties, providing valuable insights into how these systems function in different environments. The findings also have broader implications for understanding the dynamics of fields in curved space-time and the statistical behavior of quantum systems. The study is grounded on the theoretical framework of the random field and incorporates the results of the Riesz energy analysis. The investigation involves the use of mathematical models and simulation to test the hypotheses and gather data. The results are presented in a clear and concise manner, providing a straightforward summary of the key discoveries. The study contributes to the existing body of knowledge on the topic and provides a foundation for future research. The results are presented in a manner that is accessible to both specialists and non-specialists in the field. This research targets resolving secrecy concerns for nonorthogonal multiple access users by introducing an alternative decoding order method. First, we mathematically quantify the total possible decoding order options. We then propose an effective decoding order approach that guarantees positive secrecy rates for all users and, through computation, determine the feasible secure decoding order quantities. To minimize complexity in determining the best secure decoding order, we also present an efficient yet suboptimal solution method. Notably, the proposed suboptimal solution consistently achieves around 137% improvement in performance over a random secure decoding order solution.

When applying dimensionality reduction techniques to datasets with anomalies, L1-PCA has been a well-liked nonparametric method for over five decades. By using a locally optimal iterative approach to solve a nonconvex problem, several recent implementations of L1-PCA have been developed. Unfortunately, existing methods' performance can be hindered by convergence to suboptimal solutions or excessive computational demands. This paper presents an innovative variation of PCA that considers the convergence of the solution and its solution path to solutions that are consistently stable under rotational transformations. The proposed method delivers an optimized $O(\sqrt{n})$-smooth objective function iteration converging to a rotationally consistent solution with a rate of $O(1/\tau)$, where $\tau$ represents the iteration. Furthermore, it was discovered that the method can be further optimized to achieve $O(n^2)$ smoothness under certain conditions. In comparison to the optimal $O(n^2)$ smoothness achieved by the original PCA, the proposed rotationally consistent method exhibits a comparable convergence rate. Theoretical and experimental evidence supports the proposed method's superiority over existing algorithms.

Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a dataset comprised of 4000 questions expressing various emotions such as anger, gratitude, apology, sadness, and more. Our BERT-assisted labeling methodology yields a dataset of emotion-labeled questions, which we evaluate through comparative assessment using linear classifier training. The results indicate a notable 10% accuracy enhancement, thereby demonstrating the potential for language models to facilitate the annotation process.

Kopczyński and Waśkiewski enhanced the concept of energy games by integrating it with partial commutative monoids, and later focused on totally ordered groups to connect with order theory. Their work led to a fixed-point characterisation for finite games and a modal logic definition for $\nu$-translation, but their proofs lacked depth and required a more rigorous derivation. This study provides in detail the concepts of $\mu$ and $\nu$-translations for energy games over totally ordered groups, by characterising fixed points and introducing necessary game variations to establish characterisations for all variants of these games.

The subclass of magnetic Cataclysmic Variables, asynchronous polars, still lacks a comprehensive understanding. Asynchronous polars are a category of polars characterized by their white dwarf spin period differing significantly, whether longer or shorter, from their binary orbital period. The detection rate of asynchronous polars with soft X-ray emissions is disproportionate to that of hard X-ray sources, prompting the investigation of whether this discrepancy can be attributed to the characteristics of their accretion columns. Using the available data set of conventional polars, we examined the spectral properties of both hard and soft X-ray emissions for systems with synchronized, asynchronous, or near-synchronized white dwarf spins. The analysis revealed that hard X-ray spectra in asynchronous polars tend to have higher temperatures compared to their soft counterparts, but this difference is not as pronounced among systems with synchronized or near-synchronized spins. The difference between hard and soft X-ray spectra in hard sources is, however, more evident in soft sources, indicating a possible link to the spectral characteristics of asymptotic polars. The distinction between hard and soft X-ray spectra in asynchronous polars could also be a consequence of their typically higher mass transfer rates, which might account for the predominance of soft X-ray emissions among these systems.

This project's primary goal is to investigate the integration of the Reduced Basis Method (RBM) with distinct Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) approaches, namely a monolithic method and a partitioned technique. We will detail the implementation of two reduction methods and then apply them to a common test case, with a focus on a monolithic approach, solving both fluid and solid problems simultaneously, and a partitioned approach, solving these problems separately with a fixed point strategy. To evaluate these methods, we'll use a variant of the Turek-Hron benchmark test case, characterized by a fluid Reynolds number of 100.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a single robot often leads to map inconsistencies due to non-minimized drifting. Moreover, exchanging raw data with other robots to create a combined map can be time-consuming. In response, we present HiTMap, a novel mapping approach that creates a topological map hierarchy representing the unique local environment for each robot while also providing an efficient descriptor for navigation. By utilizing graph neural networks for feature extraction and pose estimation, our approach allows robots to navigate their local environments without needing to communicate with other robots. By transferring learned features to a global graph, we demonstrate that the HiTMap approach can provide accurate, drift-free navigation for a physical robot in a real-world testbed environment.

The UM-IU@LING system for the 2019 SemEval OffensEval Task is the subject of this paper. We adopted a dual-strategy to detect and classify hate speech in social media posts. For subtask A, a BERT-based classifier was adapted and achieved a high macro F1 score of 0.8236 in evaluating test data, thereby ranking 3rd among 103 competitors. Meanwhile, in subtasks B and C, a linear support vector machine was used in combination with pre-selected character n-gram features. Our method specifically for subtask C demonstrated effectiveness in identifying the victim of abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.5394, and ranked 27th out of 65 participants.

One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla.

We investigate the emergence of magnetocaloric effect (MCE) in two-dimensional transition metal dichalcogenides due to their proximity with a ferromagnetic substrate, specifically a MoTe$_2$ monolayer on EuO with a heat source. Using a tight-binding model that accounts for proximity-induced exchange and Rashba fields and temperature through Fermi statistics, we simulate this system and reveal substantial changes in spin-polarized entropy and specific heat induced by temperature and the vacuum level. By varying Rashba and exchange fields, we observe that increasing the Rashba field can lead to the closure of the valley-dependent band gap, whereas an increase in the exchange field results in proximate ferromagnetic order. As a result, a significant peak in spin-polarized entropy change can be induced by tuning these fields, in contrast to intrinsic MoTe$_2$ which lacks the MCE effect. Furthermore, our study indicates that this external control of Rashba and exchange fields can lead to highly efficient MCE at room temperature when combined with large intrinsic properties and significant valley-dependent density of states.

We investigate how electron spillover and nonlocal behavior affect light propagation between two adjacent metallic areas and compare this to a quantum hydrodynamics model. We demonstrate that a quantum hydrodynamics model which incorporates both phenomena yields accurate results, particularly as the gap narrows, in contrast to a local response model which generates unappealing results such as divergent fields and excessive energy losses. Notably, the desired limits are attained with just a minimal length equal to the Fermi wavelength.

The Calculus of Constructions, introduced in 1985 by Coquand, has been a driving force in the development of dependently typed programming and higher-order constructive logic over the past 25 years. This influential theory has influenced research in programming languages and type theory, contributing to the creation of languages such as Coq and Agda through its numerous extensions. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of the various proofs demonstrating the strong normalization property of the Calculus of Constructions, emphasizing both the underlying similarities between these proofs and the unique goals of the researchers involved.

We invite undergraduate students and early graduate students to an educational introduction to one-dimensional topological phases, focusing on the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. This will include discussions on entanglement using the correlator method and von Neumann density matrix, as well as geometric phase, polarization, and transport characteristics, all with consideration of electron-electron interactions. Hands-on numerical experiments guided by publicly available codes are used to convey the value of using topological toy models for exploring new concepts in quantum electronics.

In the case of a finite admixture model whose components and weights are both unknown, techniques from stochastic convex geometry can help us better understand how the number of components needed grows in relation to the dimension and weights. Additionally, by applying these theoretical findings, we can derive a more informative prior for nonparametric estimation based on data.

By applying a double-loop expansion within the 't Hooft-Freeman framework at four-loop order, 
we have obtained the anomalous dimension of a specific four-loop supergravity operator, 
confirming earlier findings through conventional methods. 
Notably, this operator's dimension allows for the derivation of two distinct low-lying excitations of the type-IB supergravity theory on AdS$_5$ 
$\times$ S$^5$. 
The process of expanding the relevant four-loop operator within the CM basis has yielded its two-loop correlation function components, 
which in turn facilitate the application of an established recipe to determine the operator's anom dimension, 
a procedure that extends to any loop length. 
However, this procedure necessitates the expansion of operator products in terms of the CM basis for each consecutive loop, 
a complex and time-consuming task. 
As such, we propose an alternative, more straightforward approach solely dependent on the mixing matrix's eigenvalues, 
which only depends on the operator's total dimension. 
We demonstrate the efficacy of this new method by deriving the five-loop vacuum protective operator's dimension.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, such as GPUs, has been hindered by memory management issues in object-oriented programming due to inefficient garbage collection and lack of memory control. To address these challenges, we introduce DynaSOAr, a parallel memory allocation system that supports dynamic memory operations and garbage collection within object-oriented code on GPUs. By extending C++ syntax, DynaAr allows for the creation of lightweight, garbage-collected objects with automatic and custom memory management capabilities on multiple threads and GPU cores. Implementing concurrent data structures and custom memory allocation strategies, DynaAr demonstrates automatic parallel object creation and efficient memory usage on GPUs, outperforming traditional C++ object manipulation and alternative GPU implementations, such as CUDA++ and CPODZ, in benchmarks and real-world applications.

This paper investigates the boundedness of a diverse set of operators, including those generated by the Calderón-Zygmund operators and the fractional integral operator, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces. Additionally, the article examines the boundedness of the commutators of these operators on the same space. Furthermore, specific applications are considered to obtain the boundedness of several operators, such as the Hardy-Littlewood maximal operator and the Calderón-Zygmund singular integral operators, on generalized mixed Morrey spaces.

A comprehensive theoretical framework is developed to accurately model the magnetic properties of Manganese adatoms and dimers located on the surface of Niobium, taking into consideration the influence of relativistic effects on electronic and magnetic behavior. Based on first principles, the theory predicts key parameters of Yu--Shiba--Rusinov states which arise from the interaction between the localized magnetism of the Adatom and the superconducting density of states of the metal surface. Notably, the theory correctly identifies the spin-polarization of the MR state for a single Adatom and calculates the splitting of the MR state's resonance peaks caused by this interaction. For a single Adatom, the calculated results are in good agreement with experimental and non-relativistic theoretical data. Additionally, the theory provides novel and experimentally verifiable predictions of magnetic resonances and MR state widths for a pair of parallel and antiparallel aligned Adatoms.

Our proposal, FourierMask, integrates the Fourier series with implicit neural networks to create instance segmentation masks. FourierMask uses a Fourier transformation on the coordinate positions and feeds the mapped features to an implicit function represented by a coordinate-based multi-layer perceptron (MLP). This enables FourierMask to predict specific instance masks and adapt the Fourier transformation for various objects, thus making it applicable to real-world image instances. Since implicit functions operate seamlessly over the input domain, FourierMask can generate higher-resolution masks with fewer input pixel coordinates. By integrating a renderer MLP (FourierRend), we demonstrate significant enhancements to mask quality using the predictions of FourierMask. Compared to Mask R-CNN at the same resolution, FourierMask achieves comparable performance while delivering superior results at higher resolutions.

This study examines how the discrete nature of the frequency spectrum for a non-compact manifold embedded in a higher-dimensional space affects its boundary points, focusing particularly on the Hausdorff dimension of those boundary points. Specifically, if a flat, extrinsically bounded two-dimensional surface is mapped onto a bounded, three-dimensional convex area, and the boundary points have a certain measure, the surface will have a discrete frequency spectrum. The theorem is relevant to the study of frequency spectra and has significant applications in those areas. Additionally, this study demonstrates its results by analyzing the frequency spectrum of certain closed, extrinsically bounded half-flats and confirms that some of them have discrete frequency spectra based on the frequency spectrum of their corresponding full flats. The study also introduces the concept of local boundedness for frequencies and introduces the term 'locally bounded' manifolds.

Current retrievals of cloud optical thickness and particle size using passive satellite imaging techniques fail for complex convective clouds. These failures stem from the limitation of using one-dimensional radiative transfer theory to analyze three-dimensional cloud morphologies. Cloud tomography offers a promising alternative to treating clouds as fully three-dimensional objects. Developing efficient forward solvers for three-dimensional radiative transfer will be crucial for applying this method from space. By acknowledging the existence of optically thick cloud cores, where scattered photons do not contribute useful information, we can refine future 3D retrievals. Investigating this phenomenon using data from the MISR and MODIS satellite imagers, we identified key insights to streamline cloud tomographic reconstruction. Notably, we determined the veiled core of optically thick clouds to typically be at an optical distance of around 5 from the cloud's boundary, allowing for more efficient use of computational resources and potential improvements to reconstruction algorithms.

We examine the impact of a rapidly changing laser amplitude on an electron ion plasma and discover that combining a Laguerre Gaussian laser with an elliptically polarized, chirped pulse can produce a more transparent boundary layer at a lower intensity. This phenomenon results in a more efficient transfer of energy to the plasma, generating higher energies for both electrons and ions. The optimal configuration of this multi-beam setup yields electron energies of 4.55 MeV and ion energies of 88.15 keV with just 10^19 W intensity. Furthermore, by adjusting the parameters of this setup, we are able to create a more intense proton acceleration of 34.05 keV through a process of radiation pressure.

The NASA \textit{Kepler} telescope's data are being analyzed with latest open source software to identify additional planetary systems. Using these tools, the authors discovered a new planetary system, TOI-712, comprising four planets and a stellar companion. Like many other systems, this one contains small, potentially habitable planets. However, TOI-712 stands out because its innermost worlds may still be experiencing significant growth due to their star's relatively low radiation output.

TOI-712's parent star exhibits characteristics reminiscent of young, low-mass stars with properties similar to those of the Sun, albeit at a much lower temperature and brightness. The system's planets were initially flagged by the \textit{Kepler} telescope's transit data, leading to further confirmation through analysis of the system's photometric variability and detection of additional, smaller planets using the \textit{CHEOPS} telescope.

Estimates of the system's age and planets' masses suggest TOI-712 could be around 200 million years old, making it a relatively young system. The stars and planets are likely still in a developmental phase, with TOI-692's mini-Neptune worlds experiencing significant accretion of gas and dust from their orbiting paths. As such, TOI-712 represents a unique system where the boundary between adolescent and mature planetary worlds is being crossed.

We investigated the electronic and magnetic properties of carbon and nitrogen defects within rutile TiO2, using the PBE0 hybrid functional within a periodic model. This study targeted a better understanding of the active site within TiO2 catalysis processes. We found that carbon defects form two types of electronic states based on its doping configuration, while nitrogen exhibits an unusual triangular electronic state due to its planar structure. The stability, magnetic properties, and location of these states are heavily influenced by anion-anion and cation-defect interactions. These findings highlight the significance of considering anion anion and anion cation interactions to regulate the location of d-orbitals within the valence band maximum.

This letter describes the inspiration and an analytical method for detecting the production of top-quark pairs in the Large Hadron Collider through the identification of protons emitted at the front end. I demonstrate the feasibility of identifying the semi-elastic process using a dataset of 300 inverse picobarns of data, and the fully elastic process appears inaccessible. Furthermore, I illustrate that utilizing forward proton tags enables limits on certain rare top-quark decays such as $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ which would significantly surpass the current world records.

Researchers are using the method of structure functions to determine the characteristics of turbulent flows within the intra-cluster medium. However, the implementation of this method is hindered by parameter estimations that are subject to significant measurement uncertainty. Such uncertainty can compromise the reliable inference of turbulent properties. This study focuses on quantifying the uncertainty associated with the estimation of structure functions within a simulated turbulent field and an actual galaxy cluster, RAC 25. The findings are presented in terms of coefficient of variation and confidence interval, while also considering various reconstruction techniques to improve the accuracy of estimation. The study finds that, for sufficient measurement precision, the uncertainty in structure function estimation is primarily dictated by their inherent statistical variation. The relationship between structure function estimation uncertainty and the number of measurements is found to conform to a power law. The exponent of this power law is found to be consistent across different structure functions, but its value is significantly influenced by measurement bias. The findings are summarized in a parameterized model applicable to any measurement with intrinsic statistical variation proportional to the power of scale, thereby facilitating reliable estimation of turbulent characteristics in the intra-cluster medium.

In 1993, Erdos and Galvin pioneered upper density problems within Ramsey theory, specifically the problem of identifying the highest $\lambda$ value such that in every two-edge coloring of the complete infinite graph, there exists an infinitely large, monochromatically colored subgraph resembling $F$ with an upper density of at least $\lambda$. We expand upon this research by providing a lower bound for this $\lambda$ value, with specific cases where the lower bound is equal to existing upper bounds for structures like cliques and odd cycles, and a $1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ value for triangles that surpasses the previous record.

Located at the heart of the Milky Way's bulge, the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) exhibits a complex, anisotropic star formation environment driven by its dense stellar concentration. Some regions within the CMZ display elongated structures aligned with specific directions of stellar elongation. A method known as 2D shape spectroscopy is used to quantify the degree of stellar and gas alignment, correlating shapes at various distances. By comparing the random distribution of galaxies through their redshifts, this approach distinguishes genuine spatial correlations from random occurrences. Our study calculates the 2D correlation function for infrared observations of CO in 0.3 pc wavelengths, revealing nested elliptical structures along the Galactic plane and perpendicular to it. These patterns become less distinct beyond 0.15 arcseconds due to the point spread function's influence.

This paper introduces a groundbreaking method to identify Bell's Palsy solely by analyzing a person's eye movements in a video. We have observed that patients with Bell's Palsy encounter difficulty blinking their affected eye, creating a noticeable disparity in blinking patterns between the two eyes. Building on existing research, our work exclusively focuses on eye movements rather than entire facial images. This unique approach ensures individuals' anonymity and facilitates the interpretation of Bell's Palsy's root cause. We have devised a novel metric called Blink Asymmetry Ratio, quantifying the blinking disparity between the two eyes. Our proposed system, called E-FEED (Eye-focused Evaluation of Deficiency), accurately detects Bell's Palsy with exceptional precision, sensitivity, and F1 score when evaluated using a dataset containing videos of 100 individuals, some with Bell's Palsy.

Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in (0+1)d, specifically regarding noise levels. We suggest performing measurements in the basis of total charge within the qudit system, which can significantly decrease or eliminate the negative impact of higher-order errors, particularly for qudits greater than qubits. We also demonstrate that initializing qudits to their ground states rather than in a discrete basis leads to an improvement in fidelity, resulting in better outcomes even when using non-optimal initialization methods for qubits.

Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unexplored. Our studies utilize high-intensity terahertz lasers in collaboration with dense, polarized electron targets to demonstrate the generation of densely packed, polarized positron-electron pairs. The results obtained through particle-in-cell simulations reveal the importance of spin-resolved analysis in determining the mechanisms of pair production and lead to the prediction of dense, polarized positron sources that could be achieved with currently available or near-future laser and target technologies.

Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed subset S. We have derived several key results, including a characterization of groups with a polynomial diameter for a random element S, demonstrating that groups with a polynomial diameter have many small factors that form the group in various orders. Additionally, we have demonstrated that groups with a polynomial diameter have a subexponential growth for the ball of radius R, where R is the nonnegative integer representing the distance from the identity element. We have also established that groups with a polynomial diameter have a logarithmic growth for the group itself. Furthermore, we have established that groups with a polynomial diameter have a bounded collision rate for random elements up to a certain factor. Building on this research, we have derived an upper bound for the mixing time of these groups, which grows no faster than R times the polynomial degree times the coefficient, where R is the polynomial's variable. This upper bound for the mixing time implies that these groups have a vanishing spectral gap as the group size grows.

This research develops a temperature sensing circuit that is compatible with a wide range of temperatures and operates efficiently across different supply voltages.
The proposed design utilizes a Boltzmann's thermal distribution-based method to collect temperature data, utilizing a Bistable Oscillator for precise conversion times.
Notably, a voltage-based control mechanism allows the conversion time to remain consistent, minimizing the impact of process variations and wide temperature ranges.
A 12-bit analog-to-digital conversion method is used to collect temperature readings, resulting in an extremely low power consumption and high-resolution conversion.
The temperature sensor's performance was tested using a 65nm CMOS process, demonstrating minimal variation in conversion times (standard deviation of 0.05%) and exceptional temperature resolution (0.24{\deg}C) at the lowest voltage setting (0.6V).
With a 12-bit conversion, the temperature sensor achieves the highest resolution possible, but at the cost of increased inaccuracy due to the distribution of conversion times.
To mitigate this issue, a post-processing technique is applied to improve the accuracy of temperature measurements, reducing the inaccuracy to 1.4{\deg}C.
The proposed design exhibits robust performance across a wide range of temperatures (-40{\deg}C to 85{\deg}C) and supply voltages (0.6V to 1.8V), demonstrating high efficiency and low resolution (0.24{\deg}

Long-lasting stability in the magnetic fields of Ap stars, white dwarfs, and neutron stars has been observed but the exact stellar interior conditions responsible are still unknown. Some stars or pulsars may have stable non-symmetric magnetic field configurations, while others have maintained magnetic field strength for lengths of time exceeding their age using axisymmetric configurations. To better understand what drives these stability phenomena, we applied the computational code Bifrost to analyze the magnetic field stability conditions in three different types of stars: a chemically peculiar main-sequence star, a white dwarf, and a neutron star. The code's simulations were performed in 2D vertical slices, accounting for effects such as buoyancy, magnetic tension, and the possible stratification of these stars' interiors. We specifically looked at how (i) the arrangement of convective and stable layers, as well as (ii) the axisymmetry of these stars' magnetic fields affect their stability. Our results revealed that in the case of a main sequence star with a substantial portion of its interior in a stable state, the magnetic field is generally stable across a broad spectrum of orientations. In the case of white dwarfs and neutron stars, even fully magnetic field-filled stars are oriented-axis-dependent, with some orientations exhibiting stable field behavior and others exhibiting rapid disruption. The orientation-axis-dependent stability of magnetic fields in all three types of stars is the primary aspect shared across these different stars, making it the most important factor in the overall magnetic field stability of these objects.

The functional renormalization group (FRG) technique has been proven useful for analyzing complex systems in multiple disciplines, including statistical physics and quantum field theories. In spite of its advantages, a primary drawback of the FRG approach lies in its frame's inherently non-perturbative nature, which makes the renormalization group (RG) evolution of the effective action cumbersome and computationally challenging to manage. This study proposes an innovative strategy to overcome this challenge by representing the RG evolution as a numerical fluid dynamics problem. We demonstrate the application of this method to complex QFTs in zero spatial dimensions and propose it as an effective approach for the computation of equilibrium properties of such systems. The method's efficacy is established in the case of the standard $d=3$ $O(N)$ model, where the use of this technique leads to highly precise and consistent results for the critical exponents, even with a low polynomial order. The method's potential to facilitate the computation of the RG flow for the RG-beta function of the lattice lattice $\phi^4$ theory in $d=4$ is also discussed.

Music enthusiasts still heavily depend on conventional search engines like Google for pop music, which is surprising considering how indispensable the internet has become in everyday life. Our innovative proposal is for a music-centric search engine called Pied Piper, which will serve as a comprehensive meta-search tool, allowing users to find relevant music information by searching for lyrics, song metadata, audio, or a blend of any of these options.

This PhD research focuses on exploring specific geometric constructs over Lie groupoids and differential stacks. Building on the foundations laid out in [arXiv:1609.01601, arXiv:1609.01602, arXiv:1609.01603, arXiv:1609.01604], the study establishes connections to broader concepts of geometric constructs over stacks and provides detailed examples of these architectures. Additionally, the research establishes a link between local charts of differentiable stacks and certain types of Lie groupoids.

A statistical analysis of 1.3 mm continuum cores from the Dragon infrared dark cloud reveals an interesting disparity between cores associated with molecular outflows and those that are not.  The former possess greater masses and spatial extents compared to the latter, which typically exhibit sizes under 0.15 mm.  Notably, there is a distinct group of massive cores with outflows, most of which exhibit one-dimensional velocities exceeding the local sound velocity, indicating self-gravity.  This finding implies that cores with substantial mass are more inclined to form massive stars.  Since dragon infrared dark clouds prevent the observation of new massive star formation at optical wavelengths, self-gravity in massive, gravitationally bound cores with outflows supports the existence of imminent massive star formation even in these dense regions.

Godel modal logics can be regarded as an extension of intutionistic modal logics with prelinearity. This study explores algebraic and relational semantics for Godel modal logics built upon the duality between finite Godel algebras and finite forests, a type of poset. The research considers subvarieties of basic Godel algebras with two modal operators, alongside their respective classes of forest frames, both with single and double accessibility relations. These relational structures serve as prelinear counterparts to traditional intuitionistic modal logic semantics. The study specifically examines two expansions of finite Godel algebras: the addition of Dunn axioms, common in positive classical and intutionistic logic, and the addition of Fischer Servi axioms. The research provides Jonsson-Tarski-like representation theorems for different types of finite Godel modal algebras with operators.

LiDAR point clouds offer valuable measurements for complex environmental settings, allowing for updates to digital elevation models and applications such as glacial monitoring, detecting structural changes, forest assessment, and tracking urban development. However, monitoring urban areas with high-density points of active construction and moving vehicles can be challenging. This research presents a novel approach for classifying LiDAR points in a variety of settings and determining their impact on digital elevation models. In comparison to previous methods, our approach yields more accurate results with similar computational efficiency. In tests, our system produced remarkable accuracy rates of up to 99.7% for certain classifications and 95.7% for land cover assessments.

Recurrences in positive definite functions, especially concerning the underlying space dimension, have been widely used in various applications to enhance computational efficiency of coherent states. Recent work by Beatty and Hardin revealed that certain recurrence relations result in rank-n updates, yet on the sphere S^2, the necessary condition for rank-n recurrences from the addition theorem for spherical harmonics presents a challenge. We address this challenge by developing step-wise spherical harmonic identities that facilitate n=1 recurrences, and subsequently, we establish sufficient conditions for N-valued positive definite functions on S^2, and these functions will support n=1 step-wise recursive states, which are detailed for a specific application in the context of solar imaging.

The source of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) has remained a major puzzle in high-energy astrophysics for many years. To shed light on this enigma, researchers are correlating UHECRs with high-energy neutrinos as they offer a direct and magnetically unbiased insight into cosmic ray origins. Although current datasets are too limited for conclusive findings, even small correlations can provide valuable information. A new analysis has examined the possible spatial and temporal connections between UHECRs and neutrinos produced by iceCube, based on the direction of UHECR arrival and the timing of neutrino detection relative to large astrophysical sources. The study found no significant spatial clustering beyond what's expected by chance, but did observe enhanced pre-existing sources for specific energy thresholds and a slight increase in neutrino detections within 84 days of large source catalogues, indicating potential associations. Furthermore, the research discovered that certain UHECR sources exhibit an increased likelihood of producing neutrinos and that the data can already place constraints on theoretical models of neutrino production.

The flow of complex liquids between uneven surfaces is influenced by friction, which is being investigated here for particulate-stabilized foams. A novel approach is used to analyze the friction induced by rough surfaces, allowing researchers to study the effects of normal forces and surface roughness on two foam layers in counterflow. Observations and simulations reveal a consistent pattern of friction that is relatively independent of roughness, but sensitive to the applied pressure and how the surfaces are arranged, resulting in a measurable difference in the friction experienced by the inner and outer foam layers. Notably, the study finds that the roughness of the surfaces has little effect on the friction induced, allowing for a design of a roughness-neutral model to predict the behavior of the foams.

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble approach, consisting of 11 convolutional neural networks and a Dempster-Shafer classifier. Notably, for tasks 1 and 2, we utilized a dataset containing images and metadata for seven classes across datasets A-B. Our solution involved training individual CNNs for each class, with a majority-voting mechanism used to address the class with the highest confidence. To prevent errors caused by outlier samples misclassified as the target class, we introduced a novelty detector based on deep learning and entropy. This novel component identified and excluded samples with low scores from the final decision. Ultimately, our entry secured 3rd and 4th place in tasks 1 and 2, respectively.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability, whereas the rotation-induced centrifugal force promotes stability. This study presents a non-dimensional parameter that defines a range where the inner fluid can remain contained, despite being denser than the outer fluid, by adjusting the cell's rotation speed. Furthermore, the effects of membrane elasticity on the system are explored, showing that increased elasticity expands this stability range, in addition to influencing the system's behavior near the stability range's boundary through a homoclinic bifurcation.

Building on a novel theory, microstate nonequilibrium thermodynamics, we've successfully applied it to examine the dynamics of systems undergoing expansion or contraction, despite a significant challenge. Typically, this issue arises when the phase space volume changes, resulting in distinct initial and final microstates that can't be linked by reversible processes. We've now identified a solution to this problem, specifically for systems that undergo a free expansion, and determined that the heat generated during this process can in fact be recovered. Moreover, we've discovered that the work performed during the expansion can exceed the heat generated. In addition, we thermodynamically analyze microstates before and after a sudden expansion of an isolated ideal gas.

Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures, while the detection of TMC-1 cyclopentadiene and ethynyl cyclopentadiene isotopes allows for the determination of a deuterated-to-non-deuterated ratio consistent with earlier measurements. The ethynyl cyclopentadiene benzene isotopes exhibit higher deuterated-to-non-deuterated ratios, akin to the ratios of H2O and N2H4 in TMC-1, suggesting that the CCH-containing species in TMC-1 share a common formation mechanism. The lower calculated abundances for the cyclopentadiene cyano derivative support the hypothesis that the cyclopentadiene column densities are not influenced by a downward velocity component. The findings imply that carbon-nitrogen bonded cyclic molecules may be significantly less abundant than carbon-car

However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences but also on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional attention mechanisms. To address this, a novel approach is proposed that utilizes look-ahead attention to assign significance to these target words. This approach is implemented in two ways: replacing parts of the decoder's input or assigning the generated words to an separate, parallel attention mechanism. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science.

A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs. A fundamental equation of the bulk viscous component is applied to investigate the model's behavior. The Hubble parameter, the relative expansion rate, the deceleration parameter, the relative acceleration parameter, and the relative energy density are derived and analyzed for this model. The Brans-Dicke field equations are then modified by the influence of the scalar field, and the physical properties of a Brans-Dicke universe containing the unified dark fluid are examined. The results of this study reveal that the Brans-Dicke scalar field, the dark energy density, the matter density, and the temperature are all decreasing over time in an expanding Brans-Dicke universe. This research provides a theoretical basis for the possibility of dark matter and dark energy merging into a single component in a Brans-Dicke cosmology.

In collaborative learning projects, curiosity drives individuals to gather new information and share it with their teammates. Understanding curiosity in cooperative settings is a complex challenge due to its subjective nature and reliance on both visual and other forms of communication. To tackle this issue, our research introduces a novel approach that utilizes a neural network capable of processing multiple sources of data, including eye movements and other modalities. Our model's capacity to learn from an unannotated dataset surpasses conventional methods and outperforms a unimodal model through our introduced scoring system that captures the nuances of curiosity based on various forms of communication.

Gaussian processes serve as a versatile framework for estimating unknown functions while incorporating prior knowledge about their behavior.  While multiple Gaussian process models are accessible in the context of Euclidean space, their selection is significantly more limited when working within the context of undirected graphs. This research adapts the stochastic partial differential equation formulation for Mat\'ern Gaussian processes - a popular choice for its broad applicability beyond statistics and machine learning - to enable the development of a corresponding Gaussian process model for graphs with Mat\'ern kernels.  By focusing on the existence and uniqueness of solutions for their constructed equations, this work establishes a theoretical foundation that may facilitate broader adoption of non-rigid graph-based models in applications ranging from computer vision to physics and engineering.

The effective management of urban roads relies heavily on timely and accurate real-time traffic monitoring. Currently, existing traffic monitoring systems are either costly and limited in scope, or require substantial coordination among a large number of ridesourcing vehicles. A new approach is introduced in this paper, which utilizes a single ridesourcing vehicle to perform the most cost-effective strategy for optimal urban road network monitoring. This approach models the problem mathematically, accounting for traffic conditions and costs, and formulates it using a Markov decision process. Furthermore, the paper suggests two optimization algorithms to identify the most efficient monitoring approach for various road configurations and traffic conditions. The proposed method is evaluated through simulations based on a real-world urban road network in New York City, demonstrating its effectiveness and potential for broad adoption.

Our research investigates the implications of the J/psi decay into visible and invisible neutrino pairs for field theories representing neutrino and dark matter interactions. By analyzing experimental data, we determine neutrino effective operators and validate the validity of neutrino EFT at J/psi energy levels. The study in question focuses on investigating the constraints of certain four-neutron operators, specifically those of dimension six and eight. In addition, we examine the constraints on active-sterile neutrino mixing and the mass of the neutron, validating the validity of the sterile neutrino model in light of J/psi decay observations.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods of order p with q=p stage order and demonstrate them through specific examples up to order four, further confirming their efficiency in solving non-stiff problems via numerical experiments and theoretical convergence analysis.

This work introduces multivariate functional singular spectrum analysis (MFSSA) across various dimensional domains, building on the foundations of multivariate singular spectrum analysis (MSSA). We offer a comprehensive framework consisting of theoretical underpinnings and a step-by-step implementation guide for the algorithm. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of MFSSA through comparative studies of reconstruction accuracy in multivariate functional time series (MFTS) and real-world applications, including the analysis of intraday temperature curves in Berlin over multiple years. Having the MFSSA algorithm readily available as an R package will facilitate its adoption and further development by the statistical community.

Deep learning-based automated evaluation systems (AES) are increasingly relied upon by recruitment professionals, yet the inner workings of these algorithms remain opaque to their human users. Recent studies suggest that the inner workings of these algorithms are susceptible to minor inaccuracies in the training data and data distribution shifts, which can lead to unexpected performance declines. Our investigation delves into these phenomena from the perspective of system stability, revealing that the high average performance of AES systems comes with a price of extreme sensitivity and over-stability. Our findings suggest that the susceptibility of AES systems to data noise and distribution shifts can be attributed to their operation within an extremely narrow range, characterized as both over-stable and sensitive. As a defensive measure, our proposed AEOS framework aims to enhance the robustness of AES systems by training them to function efficiently outside their average performance range, thereby mitigating the susceptibility of these systems to data noise and distribution shifts. Our proposed method addresses this issue through a series of innovations, resulting in enhanced robustness of AES systems, as evidenced by our experimental evaluations. Our results reveal significant improvements of up to 20% in accuracy across various evaluation scenarios, leading to more reliable and consistent performance of AES systems.

The power law decay $p(t,x) \sim t^{-\phi(x)}$ is a well-known characteristic of the one-dimensional simple random walk, where $p(t,x)$ denotes the probability that the probability measure $dt\delta(X_t-x)$ spent an extended period of time in an infinitesimally small interval centered at $x$ over a duration $t$, with $0<\phi(x)<1$ varying with position $x$. This phenomenon is due to non-reversible dynamics that cause the random walk to remain trapped in certain regions for prolonged periods. Notably, this universal behavior is found to apply not just to walks with fixed steps but also to walks governed by Lévy flights and variable step sizes. This study demonstrates that $p(t,x)$ also exhibits the same power law decay for VNW (Andrew's walk) variable steps, with varying step sizes, and further finds that the function $\phi(x)$ can be explicitly calculated for a broad category of step-size distributions that include the uniform distribution.

The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, and found evidence supporting the presence of helicon mode discharge based on measurements including plasma density, magnetic field distribution, and power absorption. Further analysis, involving a global model, revealed that the plasma source operates in a transition between low and high density discharges, and is not optimized for high density plasma.

In comparison to conventional chemical pesticides, microbial pesticides exhibit numerous advantages, which can be modelled through a system where entomopathogenic nematodes are used to eliminate and concurrently suppress the population of target insects. This system aims to manage pests through a continuous nematode release mechanism, where the model's equilibrium and Hopf bifurcation periodic solutions are analyzed for optimal pest control, which is further confirmed by numerical simulations and case studies.

A pathologist's task of identifying cancerous nuclei in histopathology images is significantly complicated by the intensive and fatiguing nature of the task, especially when dealing with a vast number of small and frequently clustered white blood cells. Furthermore, accurately detecting and classifying these cells requires a high level of expertise and can be further hindered by a lack of sufficient training data, often resulting in poor performance. To address these challenges, we present a novel approach that employs deep learning to assist pathologists in their analysis of histopathology images. Our proposed framework, based on a two-stage convolutional neural network and inspired by the F-LightNet architecture, allows us to efficiently process large images while maintaining a high level of accuracy in nucleus detection. By training a decoder stage on smaller sub-images, we are able to generate comprehensive maps of image features that preserve vital structural information, enabling the detection of nuclei with a high level of precision. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods, achieving a high level of sensitivity and specificity in our experiments.

Let's consider a non-Archimedean local field of characteristic not two and denote it by F. Additionally, let G be either a specific type of special orthogonal group with an odd number of dimensions or a symplectic group with a specific dimensionality, denoted as SO(2r+1)(F) or Sp(2r)(F) respectively. This paper focuses on establishing the local converse theorem for the representation of G. To this end, for two given irreducible admissible generic representations of G, with shared central character and gamma factors, our result stipulates that these representations are isomorphic. To prove this, we draw from the Cogdell, Shahidi, and Tsai framework of partial Bessel functions and the categorization of irreducible generic representations. Furthermore, our result extends the earlier work by Jiang and Soudry for representations of additive and multiplicative groups as well as even special orthogonal groups.

Xiong and Liu previously provided a characterizing criterion for graphs G whose iterated line graphs L^2(G) contain a Hamiltonian path. 
This condition was initially subject to a connectivity requirement. 
We here present a new, necessary and sufficient condition for a graph G to be such that its iterated line graph L^2(G) includes a Hamiltonian path, via an exact countable condition. 
This new condition is expressed in terms of two parameters of the graph G - its vertex set and edge set path cover numbers, denoted respectively as cpv(G) and cpe(G) and related details. 
Our finding thus refines previous related results, particularly those regarding the hamiltonian path index of graphs.

Cell death due to pyroptosis, characterized by swelling and inflammation, can contribute to the high rate of pulmonary inflammation in severe COVID-19 cases.  Pyroptosis, initiated by the SARS-CoV-2 protease main chymotrypsin-like protease (M^pro), is a complex process that involves multiple stages, from initial recognition to the formation of gasdermin-D pores and the release of inflammatory contents.  Understanding the effects of anti-inflammatory medications, such as methylprednisolone, on this process is crucial, as they may exacerbate pyroptotic cell death by limiting the cell's ability to clear toxic GSDMD proteins and cellular waste, thus preventing methylprednisolone's anti-inflammatory effects and promoting cell death.  Our single-cell ordinary differential equation (ODE) model dissects pyroptosis at a granular level, allowing us to observe how methylprednisolone's limited ability to internalize GSDMD and the cell cycle's disruption contributes to pyroptotic cell death.

External influences such as sensor malfunctions or unanticipated environmental changes can hinder an agent's performance in a learning task by introducing unknown state variables and associated rewards. Sometimes, these variables are unnecessary for successful task completion, but their presence can make it difficult for the agent to discover an optimal solution. Furthermore, unexpected rewards from these variables can mislead the agent. In this paper, we investigate the problem of identifying and eliminating these unwanted variables and rewards. Our key contribution is a novel framework for an agent to identify these variables on its own, along with a set of algorithms enabling the agent to learn an optimal solution in the absence of these variables and rewards. Sensor malfunctions or environmental factors can make certain variables and their associated rewards inaccessible to the agent, thus we model this scenario as a partially observable Markov decision process and a corresponding hierarchical structure, along with a stochastic reward system. Our algorithms use two distinct approaches to learn a policy in this framework, including multi-task reinforcement learning and curiosity-driven exploration, thus we prove convergence to the best possible solution in this hierarchical setting, thus our results show that the agent can successfully ignore these unwanted variables and rewards, thus we prove that the agent can converge to the optimal policy in the absence of these variables and rewards.
